# California Proposition 45 and CEQA: What It Would Change for Neighbors, Owners and Developers

California voters will decide on November 3, 2026 whether to adopt Proposition 45, the "Building an Affordable California Act." Its official ballot title is "Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute." If it passes, it would add a new chapter to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), Public Resources Code Sections 21010 through 21034. For projects it calls "essential," it would set deadlines for environmental review, limit the alternatives an environmental impact report must study, and narrow both the claims and the remedies available in a CEQA lawsuit.

This article explains what the measure's text says, not whether to vote for it. It is written for the people most likely to end up in a California courtroom over it: neighbors and homeowners associations that challenge projects, and property owners and developers who propose them. Because it is a ballot measure, every statement below is about what Proposition 45 would do if approved. We will update this page after the election.

Key takeaways

*   California Proposition 45 (November 3, 2026) is an initiative statute that would add Public Resources Code Sections 21010 to 21034 to CEQA; it does not exempt projects from environmental review, and under proposed Section 21014 public agencies keep their discretion to approve or deny.
*   Proposition 45's procedures are generally optional for the project applicant: proposed Public Resources Code Section 21015(a) lets an applicant for an "essential project" use "none, some, or all" of the new chapter, so a neighbor or city cannot invoke it on its own.
*   For essential projects whose applicants opt in, proposed Section 21018 would require a California local agency to decide whether to certify an environmental impact report within 365 business days, and whether to adopt a negative declaration within 180 business days, counted from the date the application is determined or deemed complete.
*   A CEQA lawsuit against an essential project whose applicant opts into Proposition 45 would generally have to be filed within 30 days after the notice of determination or notice of exemption is filed, would be limited to claims that the agency violated "objective existing laws," and would be directed to be completed within 270 days including appeals (proposed Sections 21026 and 21027).
*   Under proposed Section 21027(c), a California court that finds a CEQA violation on an opted-in essential project could not order the agency to rescind its approval; the writ remedy would be limited to barring the noncompliant part, phase or activity from starting until the violation is corrected, with a narrow injunction exception for proven public safety impacts (Section 21027(e)(1)).

## What is California Proposition 45, and which projects count as "essential"?

Proposition 45 is a November 2026 California initiative statute that would add a new CEQA chapter for "essential projects." Under proposed Public Resources Code Section 21013, those are essential housing, clean energy, water, public health, public safety, broadband, education facility and transportation projects. Each category has its own definition and exclusions in proposed Section 21028.

### Essential housing is broad

Proposed Section 21028(l) lists nine kinds of essential housing project:

1.  Residential units only.
2.  Mixed-use development meeting the residential-share tests in Section 21028(y).
3.  Transitional, emergency shelter or supportive housing.
4.  Farmworker housing.
5.  Group living accommodations.
6.  Student housing.
7.  Senior housing, if it also qualifies as a "housing development project" under Government Code Section 65589.5(h)(2).
8.  Subdivisions or common interest developments of residential units or unimproved residential lots.
9.  Conversion of an existing commercial building to residential use.

A mixed-use project qualifies under Section 21028(y) if at least two-thirds of its new or converted square footage is residential, or if it meets one of two alternative tests that require at least 50 percent residential square footage, at least 500 net new units, no hotel or other transient lodging, and, for the second test, additional demolition and conversion thresholds. The nonresidential portion cannot include heavy industrial, extractive, port, refinery or hazardous materials uses.

Some commercial-to-residential conversions already have their own state pathways with different CEQA treatment; our article on [retail-to-residential conversions](/blog/california-retail-to-residential-conversion/) explains how AB 2011 and SB 6 differ.

### What is excluded

Proposed Section 21028(m)(2) excludes, across every category, a project that includes a jail or other detention facility and a project involving a new oil or natural gas production facility. Individual categories carry their own exclusions: Delta conveyance facilities are excluded from water projects, nuclear generation from clean energy, and high-speed rail components from transportation.

The measure's housing definition does not contain the conditions California's 2025 CEQA housing exemption uses. Public Resources Code Section 21080.66, added by AB 130 (Chapter 22, Statutes of 2025) and later amended, exempts qualifying housing only if, among other things, the site is generally 20 acres or less (with a smaller four-acre cap for some projects, including builder's remedy projects), is in an urban or infill location, is consistent with the general plan and zoning, and avoids the sensitive-site exclusions in Government Code Section 65913.4(a)(6). Because Proposition 45 does not create an exemption, it does not include those limits; it changes the procedure for projects that still go through review. Proposed Section 21014(e)(1) states that the new chapter does not limit any existing statutory or categorical exemption.

Proposition 45 also does not rezone land. It changes how CEQA review and CEQA litigation work. Whether a project complies with the zoning code, the general plan or the Housing Accountability Act is a separate question under separate law. Some state laws already take qualifying projects outside CEQA review through ministerial approval, as our article on [SB 79 transit upzoning](/blog/sb-79-transit-upzoning-what-california-property-owners-can-do/) explains.

### It is opt-in

Under proposed Section 21015(a), "an applicant may elect to utilize none, some, or all of the provisions of this chapter." A developer that prefers the existing CEQA process can keep it. Tribal consultation under proposed Section 21016 is mandatory for any project that uses the chapter at all, and it is limited to federally recognized tribes that are traditionally and culturally affiliated with the project's geographic area (Section 21028(e)). The measure states that its deadlines do not shorten consultation under existing Sections 21080.3.1 and 21080.3.2.

The measure does not expressly say whether the litigation limits in proposed Sections 21026 and 21027 depend on that election; Section 21026(a)(1) refers to "any action or proceeding" challenging an essential project's approval, so expect that question to be argued.

## How fast would a California city have to finish CEQA review under Prop 45?

For an opted-in essential project, proposed Public Resources Code Section 21018 sets four deadlines for a California local agency, all in business days and all running from the date the application is determined or deemed complete: 30 to choose the review track, 365 to decide on an environmental impact report, 180 for a negative declaration, and 90 for an exemption or addendum.

### Completeness comes first

Under proposed Section 21017, the agency has 30 calendar days from receipt to decide whether an application is complete; if it does not act, the application "shall be deemed complete for the purposes of this division." An incompleteness letter must include an "exhaustive written corrections list," and the agency may not later add new items. The applicant has 90 days to resubmit, and may appeal an incompleteness finding, with a decision due within 60 days; these periods are calendar days.

### The review clock

| Step (Prop 45, if approved)                                            | Proposed section | Time | Unit          | Runs from                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | ---- | ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Completeness decision                                                  | 21017(a)(2)      | 30   | calendar days | Agency's receipt of application                                                                             |
| Choose review track                                                    | 21018(a)         | 30   | business days | Application determined or deemed complete                                                                   |
| Decide whether to certify an EIR                                       | 21018(b)         | 365  | business days | Same                                                                                                        |
| Decide on a negative declaration or mitigated negative declaration     | 21018(c)         | 180  | business days | Same                                                                                                        |
| Exemption, prior evaluation or addendum                                | 21018(d)         | 90   | business days | Same                                                                                                        |
| Hearing after a missed deadline                                        | 21020(b)         | 60   | calendar days | Agency's receipt of the applicant's written request                                                         |
| Applicant's suit over a missed deadline, denial or unlawful conditions | 21020(g)         | 90   | calendar days | The agency's failure, denial or imposition of conditions (the measure does not say when a "failure" occurs) |

Proposed Section 21028(f) defines "day" as a business day for Sections 21018 and 21019 only; everywhere else in the chapter, a day is a calendar day. Section 21019 sets parallel deadlines for state and other nonlocal agencies. Under Section 21018(e), the review deadlines "shall be extended upon written request from the applicant."

### A missed deadline is not an approval

Proposition 45 contains no "deemed approved" rule. If the agency misses a deadline, the applicant may request a hearing in writing, and within 60 days of receiving the request the agency must hold a meeting or hearing before its highest-ranking decision-making body (or, if it has none, its highest-ranking official or designee) and make final written determinations on the environmental document and on whether to approve or disapprove the project (proposed Section 21020(b)). The measure calls these deadlines a "nondiscretionary ministerial duty," enforceable by the applicant in court. The agency can still say no. ROMO has written separately about California's existing [permit delay and deemed-approved remedies](/blog/california-permit-delay-remedies-deemed-approved/), which work differently.

### What the study must cover

Proposed Section 21022 directs that impacts be identified, judged and mitigated "based on compliance with existing laws," defined in Section 21028(r) as laws formally adopted and in effect when the application was submitted, with exceptions for a specific, adverse life-safety impact and for building and fire code updates that take effect before a stated point. An applicant may also elect to lock in the significance thresholds the agency had published, adopted or routinely used.

Under proposed Section 21025, an environmental impact report for an essential project that "complies with this article" would analyze three alternatives: the project, one alternative the applicant develops, and no project. That limit is tied to the optional pre-application scoping process in Section 21024, so it is not automatic for every opted-in project.

## Could neighbors and HOAs in California still sue under CEQA if Prop 45 passes?

Yes. Proposition 45 would not bar CEQA lawsuits, but for opted-in essential projects it would shorten the filing deadline to 30 days from a notice of determination or exemption, limit claims to violations of "objective existing laws," limit the record, direct completion within 270 days including appeals, and bar courts from ordering an approval rescinded.

### Comments must be in on time

This change may most directly affect a California neighbor or homeowners association. Under proposed Section 21021, comment periods would be 20 calendar days for a negative declaration and 45 calendar days for a draft environmental impact report, and they "shall not be tolled or extended except by a court of competent jurisdiction." Only listed categories of comments enter the administrative record: comments received during the comment period, comments received at least 48 hours before a hearing or decision where no comment period applies, oral testimony at a noticed and recorded hearing, and, at a hearing or appeal on a CEQA determination, comments received at least 48 hours before it that raise issues which could not have been raised earlier because of significant project changes or new information. "All other public comments shall be disregarded and excluded from the administrative record."

In practice, a neighbor who waits until the city council hearing to submit a new written objection may find it excluded from the record; oral testimony at a noticed and recorded hearing is listed as part of the record, but how courts will treat issues raised only at that stage is not yet known. Under existing CEQA, Public Resources Code Section 21177 already requires most issues to be raised before the agency decides (see the exhaustion discussion on our [zoning disputes page](/zoning-disputes/)), and how courts would reconcile that rule with the new record limits is also open.

### What a lawsuit could claim

Proposed Section 21026(b)(1) states that "a petitioner's claims shall be limited to a public agency's noncompliance with objective existing laws." "Objective" is defined as involving no personal or subjective judgment and being uniformly verifiable against an external and uniform benchmark or criterion knowable by both the applicant and the agency before the application was submitted. Under Section 21026(c)(1), "the court shall only determine whether the approval or authorization is supported by substantial evidence" in light of the whole record. Claims about public participation succeed only if the failure was arbitrary and capricious and caused prejudicial error.

How a court applies an "objective existing laws" limit to CEQA, a statute that calls for many judgment-based analyses, is an open question. No court has interpreted these provisions, and the outcome of the first cases is hard to predict.

### Deadlines and the 270-day target

| Litigation step                    | Current CEQA                                          | Prop 45, essential project (if approved)                                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| File after notice of determination | 30 days (Pub. Resources Code Sec. 21167(b), (c), (e)) | 30 days (proposed Sec. 21027(a)(1)(A))                                                                                                                                                   |
| File after notice of exemption     | 35 days (Sec. 21167(d))                               | 30 days (proposed Sec. 21027(a)(1)(A))                                                                                                                                                   |
| Complete the case                  | No fixed statewide limit for most projects            | "Within 270 days, inclusive of original and appellate court proceedings," with up to 90 more days by the court; any other extension requires consent of petitioner, agency and applicant |

The measure does not say when the 270 days begins or what happens if a court cannot finish in time. Proposition 45 also does not say what deadline applies when no notice is filed; existing Section 21167 generally allows 180 days in that situation, as summarized in the deadlines table in our [builder's remedy article](/blog/california-builders-remedy-housing-element-lawsuits/).

In Los Angeles County, local agencies file notices of determination, and any notices of exemption they choose to file, with the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk, and the filing date is what starts the clock. Check the county's posted CEQA notices rather than relying on the date of a city council vote.

### What a court could order

Under proposed Section 21027(c), a court that finds a violation would issue a writ identifying the specific deficiency and the affected part, phase or activity. "The remedy shall be limited only to prohibiting commencement of the noncomplying part, phase, or activity" until the violation is corrected, and the court "may not order or direct" an agency to "rescind its approval or authorization of the essential project." Under Section 21027(e)(1), an injunction is available only on clear and convincing evidence of a specific, adverse public safety impact with no feasible mitigation, and only for that component.

That is a significant change for neighbors. Under current CEQA, the Legislative Analyst's Office notes, a court can halt an entire project. Under Proposition 45, the rest of the project could proceed while the noncompliant piece is fixed, and once the return to the writ is accepted, Section 21027(d) would bar further CEQA challenges to the project's implementation.

California law already places some limits on challenges to housing projects. A challenge to a qualifying housing project can carry bond exposure under Code of Civil Procedure Section 529.2, which we covered in our article on [SB 1344 and housing project lawsuit bonds](/blog/california-housing-project-lawsuit-bond-sb-1344/). For projects that fall under the Housing Accountability Act, our guide to [builder's remedy lawsuits](/blog/california-builders-remedy-housing-element-lawsuits/) explains what neighbors can still challenge.

## If Prop 45 passes, when does it take effect, and what happens to pending California projects?

An initiative statute takes effect on the fifth day after the California Secretary of State files the statement of the vote (Cal. Const., art. II, sec. 10(a)); the Secretary of State's calendar sets December 11, 2026 for certifying the statement of vote. Proposed Section 21033 would apply the measure on its effective date to "all pending and future" agency and judicial review of essential projects.

### Pending applications

Under proposed Section 21014(f), an applicant with a pending application not yet finally approved may withdraw and resubmit after the effective date to use the new chapter. A resubmitted housing project keeps vested rights that relate back to its original preliminary application or vesting date. An application already deemed complete stays complete. Separately, proposed Section 21014(g) applies the new timelines to any application determined or deemed complete after the effective date, whenever it was submitted.

### Pending lawsuits

Proposed Section 21026(a)(2) states that the litigation article applies to actions "pending on" or commenced after the effective date. A Los Angeles neighborhood group already in a CEQA suit against a project that qualifies as essential should expect the developer to argue that the new limits apply to the case. Whether the measure can change the rules for pending cases in every respect is likely to be litigated.

### Can the Legislature change it?

Under proposed Section 21034, the Legislature could amend the chapter by a two-thirds vote of each house, and only if an amendment is consistent with the chapter and "furthers the purposes of" it. Proposed Section 21030 declares the subject a matter of statewide concern, which bears on whether charter cities such as Los Angeles may vary its procedures.

### The fiscal estimate

The Legislative Analyst's Office estimates that initial state and local costs "likely would be in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually," with fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits partly covering them, and with uncertain longer-term effects that depend on how many projects are built.

### What to do now

If you own property in California with a pending or planned project, or you are watching one go forward next door, the useful steps are the same either way the vote goes: keep a dated record of every notice, comment and hearing, submit comments in writing within the published comment period, and calendar every filing deadline from the date the notice is actually filed. ## Common questions

What is California Proposition 45 on the November 2026 ballot?

Proposition 45, the Building an Affordable California Act, is an initiative statute that would add Public Resources Code Sections 21010 to 21034 to the California Environmental Quality Act. For essential housing, clean energy, water, public health, public safety, broadband, education facility and transportation projects whose applicants opt in, it would set review deadlines and narrow CEQA lawsuits. It does not exempt projects from environmental review.

Would Prop 45 stop neighbors from suing under CEQA in California?

No. Proposition 45 would not bar CEQA lawsuits. For an essential project whose applicant opts in, a suit would generally have to be filed within 30 days after the notice of determination or exemption is filed, claims would be limited to noncompliance with objective existing laws, and the case would be directed to be completed within 270 days including appeals.

Could a California court overturn a project approval under Prop 45?

Not by ordering the approval rescinded, if the applicant opted in. Under proposed Public Resources Code Section 21027(c), the court could only bar the specific noncompliant part, phase or activity from starting until the agency corrects the violation. An injunction would require clear and convincing evidence of a specific, adverse public safety impact with no feasible mitigation.

Does Prop 45 apply to housing projects in Los Angeles?

It could, if the project fits the measure's definition of essential housing and the applicant elects to use the new chapter. Unlike the 2025 infill housing exemption in Public Resources Code Section 21080.66, Proposition 45 does not require zoning consistency, an infill site or a maximum site size. It also does not change the zoning; it changes CEQA review and CEQA litigation.

When would Prop 45 take effect if voters approve it?

An initiative statute takes effect on the fifth day after the California Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, which the Secretary of State's calendar sets for December 11, 2026; the measure would take effect five days after that filing, not on the filing date itself. The measure states that it would then apply to all pending and future agency and judicial review of essential projects.

 **California Proposition 45**, the **Expedited Environmental Review Process for Certain Projects Initiative**, is on the [ballot](/California_2026_ballot_propositions "California 2026 ballot propositions") in [California](/California "California") as an [initiated state statute](/Initiated_state_statute "Initiated state statute") on [November 3, 2026](/California_2026_ballot_propositions "California 2026 ballot propositions").[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

A "**yes**" vote supports this initiative to make changes to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to:

*   establish deadlines for public agencies to complete environmental review and take required actions for projects deemed *essential* under the law;
*   limit public agencies' existing requirement to consider a range of project alternatives to reduce environmental impacts; and
*   change the court review process for project approvals by setting deadlines for filing and resolving lawsuits and limiting the evidence and relief the court can consider and order.

A "**no**" vote opposes this initiative to make changes to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), which governs state and local government agencies' review process for determining potential environmental impacts and mitigation solutions of proposed construction projects.

## Overview

### How would the initiative change the timelines for California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and Permit Streamlining Act (PSA) reviews?

*See also: [Measure design](#Measure_design)*

The initiative would amend the [California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)](#California_Environmental_Quality_Act_\(CEQA\)) and the [Permit Streamlining Act](#Permit_Streamlining_Act) by shortening the review process for a defined set of essential projects — housing, water systems (excluding Delta conveyance), clean energy, medical facilities, public safety infrastructure (excluding jails/prisons), broadband, education, and transportation (excluding high-speed rail).[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

Agencies would have 30 days to determine whether an application is complete, covering environmental review, permitting, and court proceedings. If no determination is made within that window, the application is automatically deemed complete. This would apply even when local general plan or zoning changes are required. The 30-day rule would apply to both lead agencies (the agency principally responsible for approving the project) and responsible agencies (other public agencies with a role in approval).[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

The initiative would shift environmental review and permitting timelines from calendar days to business days and require lead agencies to issue permit decisions at the same time as the environmental review, rather than after. If agencies miss deadlines, applicants can grant more time to the agency or request a hearing. The initiative would also authorize applicants to challenge adverse decisions in court and require that such challenges be resolved within 270 days (with a possible 90-day extension).[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

### How would the initiative change the environmental review process?

*See also: [Measure design](#Measure_design)*

The initiative would limit public comment periods for essential project environmental impact reports (EIRs) to 45 days. Currently, state law sets a minimum rather than a maximum. It would require a court order to extend that window. It would also establish an optional preliminary scoping process in which applicants meet with the lead agency to discuss the project and potential impacts, after which the applicant may develop a single alternative for EIR consideration. Currently, state law requires agencies to develop and evaluate a range of alternatives. Additionally, agencies would be required to base their environmental impact evaluations on existing laws and the significance thresholds in place at the time of application, rather than applying varying or project-specific thresholds as currently permitted.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

The EIR process also includes a tribal consultation component. The initiative would require applicants and lead agencies to consult with native tribes listed as federally recognized, not the state Native American Heritage Commission list. It would also require applicants to be screened by the lead agency and by tribes that may be affected by the project's impacts on their cultural resources. A good-faith tribal consultation would also be a prerequisite for lead agency approval.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

### Who supports and opposes the initiative?

*See also: [Support](#Support) and [Opposition](#Opposition)*

[Committee to Build an Affordable California](#Support) is leading the Yes on Prop 45 campaign. Associated General Contractors of California, California Building Industry Association, California Business Roundtable, California Chamber of Commerce, California Hospital Association, and California Water Association endorsed the initiative. The committees surrounding the campaign reported over $70 million in contributions through September 19. Jennifer Barrera, president and CEO of the California Chamber of Commerce, said, "Californians have too long paid the price for bureaucratic red tape and delays, and they’re ready for solutions. Reaching this milestone early shows voters are eager to modernize the project approval process so we can build what we need, bring costs down, and make California more affordable. We can protect the environment and good-paying jobs while delivering the essential projects California urgently needs."[\[2\]](#cite_note-support-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) 

[People Over Polluters](#Opposition) is leading the No on Prop 45 campaign. The committees surrounding the campaign reported more than $15 million in contributions. Democratic Party of California, California Federation of Teachers, California Professional Firefighters, ACLU of Southern California, Clean Water Action, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, the Sierra Club of California oppose the initiative. Miguel Miguel, director of Sierra Club California, said, "We strongly oppose it. We know that what they are really trying to do is eliminate a lot of the environmental safeguards that have existed for a long time. People have to read long technical documents to get a better understanding of whether a project is right or wrong for their community. It takes time for us to do discovery and have conversations with neighbors. Our input needs to be valued. Are developers trying to make it efficient or cut out the true voices of people who have concerns?”[\[4\]](#cite_note-4)

Essential projects definition

The initiative would make changes to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and Permit Streamlining Act (PSA) as it relates to essential projects. Essential projects would include the following list of projects and associated infrastructure:

*   housing,
*   water systems (excluding Delta conveyance facilities),
*   clean energy,
*   medical treatment facilities,
*   public safety (including first responder facilities and wildfire risk reduction; excluding jails or prisons),
*   broadband internet access,
*   education facilities, and
*   transportation (excluding high-speed rail).

  
 

Essential project applicants using the process proposed by the initiative would also be subject to certain labor requirements. The initiative would allow applicants who submitted applications prior to the implementation of the initiative to withdraw their applications and resubmit according to the new process.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)[\[5\]](#cite_note-lao-5)

Changes to CEQA and PSA time limits

The initiative would set a 30-day time limit for lead or responsible agencies to determine whether an essential project application is complete. This would apply to projects needing local general plan or zoning changes. If the lead or responsible agency does not make a determination within 30 days, the application is automatically considered complete. A lead agency is defined in CEQA as "public agency which has the principal responsibility for carrying out or approving a project." A responsible agency is a "public agency which proposes to carry out or approve a project, for which a lead agency is preparing or has prepared an EIR or negative declaration."[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

  
 The initiative would change environmental review timelines by using business days instead of calendar days. It would extend the time limit from 90 calendar days to 90 business days for lead agencies to determine if the project is exempt from an environmental review. If the agency does not meet the established time limit, the applicant may either grant the agency more time or request a meeting or hearing within 60 days and require the agency to approve or deny the project at the meeting.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)  
 The initiative would also require a lead agency to make its permit decisions at the same time as its environmental review or determine that the project is exempt from environmental review. A responsible agency would be required to make permit decisions either 90 days from determining the application is complete or within one day of the lead agency approving the overall project, whichever is later. If an agency misses a deadline, the applicant would be authorized to grant more time or request a meeting or hearing that must be held within 45 days, where the agency must report its final decision. The initiative would authorize applicants to challenge adverse decisions in court.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)  
 

For court proceedings, the initiative would require that they be resolved within 270 days, with an optional court extension of 90 days.

Changes to environmental review

The initiative would change the environmental review process under CEQA for essential projects. It would limit the number of days an agency provides for public comment to 45 days for an environmental impact report (EIR). The initiative would also require a court order to extend the public comment period. Currently, state law sets a minimum number of days for the public comment period.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)[\[5\]](#cite_note-lao-5)

  
 The initiative would also allow essential project applicants to opt into a preliminary scoping process that allows the applicant to meet with the lead agency and provide information to discuss the project, potential environmental impacts, and alternatives to mitigate environmental impact. After participating in the scoping process, the applicant would be allowed to develop a single project alternative that may be considered during the preparation of the EIR. Currently, the lead agency is required to develop and consider a range of alternatives to mitigate environmental impact.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)[\[5\]](#cite_note-lao-5)  
 The initiative would require public agencies evaluating the project's environmental impact to base their evaluation on compliance with existing laws and on the "thresholds of significance" adopted or used by the agency at the time of application. Currently, agencies are authorized to use various impact thresholds throughout the review and application process, including project-specific thresholds.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)[\[5\]](#cite_note-lao-5)  
 

The initiative would make changes to the process by which applicants consult native tribes about potential projects. It would require applicants and lead agencies to consult with native tribes listed as federally recognized and not the state Native American Heritage Commission list. It would also require applicants to be screened by the lead agency and tribes that may experience effects to their cultural resources by the project. This would include developing ways to mitigate impacts that would be included as an enforceable requirement of the project. The initiative would also require essential project applicants to conduct a "good-faith" consultation" with tribes to be approved by a lead agency.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

Changes to judicial review

The initiative would increase the legal standard that courts use when reviewing challenges to a lead agency's authorization or environmental review. A challenge to the approval of an essential project would be "limited to whether the approval or authorization complies objective existing laws." The initiative would limit the *administrative record*, information used in CEQA cases, to documents the lead agency is required to make public, public comments and responses, and an applicant's response to the lead agency's questions about project compliance. Currently, the court can use independent judgment to determine an agency's compliance with CEQA.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)[\[5\]](#cite_note-lao-5)

  
 

The initiative would also limit how a court delays or stops a project. The initiative would not allow a court to rescind project approval if the court determines the agency's approval does not comply with CEQA. The initiative would allow the court to stop the part of the project that is not in compliance with CEQA or that poses a public safety risk, but only until it is corrected. The initiative would also prohibit other parts of the project from being challenged if they were not in the original court order. The initiative would also prohibit later challenges, from implementation to construction, if the agency's project approval was not challenged.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)[\[5\]](#cite_note-lao-5)

A prediction market is a platform where users buy and sell contracts tied to the outcome of future events. The price of a contract reflects the market's estimated probability of that outcome — a contract priced at 55 cents suggests the market estimates a 55 percent chance the event occurs. Volume reflects how actively a market is being traded.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) Unlike polls, which survey a sample of voters, prediction markets aggregate the financial stakes of individual bettors. A market with higher trading volume is generally considered more reliable than one with low volume, though prices can be influenced by large individual traders.

### Substantial Evidence Standard vs. Fair Argument
Under current CEQA, the **fair argument standard** applies to whether an EIR is required (vs. a negative declaration or mitigated negative declaration): if there is a “fair argument” based on substantial evidence that a project *may* have a significant environmental effect, an EIR is needed. This is a relatively low, non-deferential threshold that favors more analysis. For reviewing the *adequacy* of a completed EIR, courts use the more deferential **substantial evidence** standard (upholding the agency if there is substantial evidence in the record supporting its conclusions).

Prop 45 would **eliminate the fair argument standard** for essential projects and apply the deferential **substantial evidence standard** to judicial review of *all* CEQA documents (EIRs, NDs, and MNDs). Claims would be limited to a public agency’s “noncompliance with objective existing laws.” Courts would determine whether the approval is supported by substantial evidence in light of the whole record, with a higher bar for challengers and more deference to the agency. This makes it harder to force an EIR or successfully challenge a document.[[2]](https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-45-environmental-review-ceqa)

### Frozen Thresholds, Significance Determination, Vest Existing Laws
**Significance** of impacts would be determined *solely* based on whether the project violates “existing laws”—formally adopted legal requirements in statutes, regulations, rules, standards, or ordinances that were in effect on the date the application was submitted. Agencies generally could not apply later-updated standards or new scientific information (with a limited exception for life-safety/building/fire code updates). Only adopted, **objective** thresholds (uniformly verifiable against an external benchmark, involving no personal/subjective judgment, and knowable in advance) tied to those legal requirements could be used. This “freezes” thresholds at application time.[[3]](https://ascent.inc/proposition-45/)

Upon filing, the project **vests** into those existing laws and standards. Applicants could also elect to “vest into” any significance thresholds the agency had previously published, adopted, or routinely used, and the agency could not override that. This locks in the rules as of the application date, reducing agencies’ ability to update reviews based on new information or evolving science.[[4]](https://www.smwlaw.com/2026/10/06/proposition-45-what-public-agencies-need-to-know/)

### Only Mitigation (Limited Scope and Alternatives)
The process would focus environmental review on identifying, judging, and **mitigating** impacts based on compliance with those frozen existing objective laws, rather than a broader CEQA-style analysis of all potential effects, cumulative impacts, or evolving concerns.
